questions.question: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC — which API style to pick and when?
questions.title: API Styles: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC
questions.direct_answer: Three dominant API styles, each with distinct sweet spots: **REST/JSON** is the ubiquitous default — resource-based, HTTP verbs, cacheable, human-readable, universal tooling; weak schemas without OpenAPI; can be verbose and chatty. **GraphQL** — client picks exactly the fields they need in one request, eliminates over/under-fetching, powerful dev experience; server complexity (query planners, N+1 risk, harder caching). **gRPC** — HTTP/2 + Protobuf, binary, compact, fast, polyglot; best for internal service-to-service; limited browser support without proxy. Rule: REST for public APIs and simple services, GraphQL for mobile/complex frontends where field selection matters, gRPC for high-performance internal RPC.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding when each API style excels; modern API design pragmatism
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Blindly using REST for everything; adopting GraphQL without understanding N+1 and caching complexity; using gRPC for public APIs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss over/under-fetching, persisted queries, BFF pattern, HTTP caching vs GraphQL caching, Apollo Federation vs REST microservices, Protobuf schema evolution

sections.title: Three API Philosophies
sections.content:
In 2026, three API styles dominate production systems:

**REST (HTTP + JSON)** Resource-based: URLs identify things (`/users/42`), verbs act on them (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE).
- JSON is human-readable.
- Tooling is everywhere (curl, Postman, browsers, every language).
- HTTP semantics (status codes, caching, content negotiation) are free.
- Schemas exist via OpenAPI but are optional. Scales from tiny to massive.

Downsides: verbose payloads (JSON text), multiple round-trips for complex views (one call for user, one for their orders, one for each order's items), over-fetching (returns fields client doesn't need), under-fetching (missing nested data).

**GraphQL (Facebook, open-sourced 2015)**
Single endpoint accepting a query language. Client specifies exactly what data it wants: fields, nested relations, arguments. One request returns exactly that shape. Strong schema (SDL); introspection; rich tooling (GraphiQL, Apollo Studio).

Downsides: query cost unpredictable (complex queries can hammer backend), N+1 problem without DataLoader, HTTP caching broken (POST with body), server-side complexity, harder to rate-limit, learning curve.

**gRPC (Google, 2015)**
HTTP/2 + Protobuf. Binary, compact (3–10x smaller than JSON), fast serialization. Strongly typed schemas generate client/server stubs in multiple languages. Four RPC modes: unary, server-streaming, client-streaming, bidirectional. Deadlines, metadata, interceptors.

Downsides: not browser-friendly (needs gRPC-Web proxy like Envoy), harder debugging (binary wire), schema discipline required.

**Which for what?**
- **REST**: public APIs, B2B, mobile/web where simplicity wins, Spring Boot defaults
- **GraphQL**: complex frontends (mobile, SPA) where mobile bandwidth and many queries matter
- **gRPC**: internal microservices; service-to-service at high volume; polyglot teams

Real architectures often combine all three: REST at the edge; GraphQL as a BFF for mobile; gRPC between internal services.

sections.title: Feature Comparison
sections.content:
| Dimension | REST | GraphQL | gRPC |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Transport** | HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 | HTTP POST (usually) | HTTP/2 required |
| **Encoding** | JSON, XML | JSON | Protobuf (binary) |
| **Schema** | Optional (OpenAPI) | Strong (SDL) | Strong (Protobuf) |
| **Endpoints** | Many (resource URLs) | One `/graphql` | One per service, many methods |
| **Over-fetching** | Common | Eliminated | Controlled (field masks) |
| **Under-fetching** | Common | Eliminated | N/A (request specifies) |
| **Round trips** | Often multiple | Usually one | Multiple but fast |
| **Caching** | HTTP cache native | Hard (POST + custom) | No HTTP cache |
| **Streaming** | SSE / WebSocket (ad hoc) | Subscriptions (WebSocket) | Native (4 modes) |
| **Browser support** | Native | Native (over HTTP) | Needs gRPC-Web proxy |
| **Tooling** | Postman, curl, everything | GraphiQL, Apollo Studio | grpcurl, Buf, less ubiquitous |
| **Learning curve** | Low | Medium | Medium-High |
| **Server complexity** | Low-Medium | High (resolvers, DataLoader) | Medium |
| **Client complexity** | Low (just fetch) | Medium (queries + cache) | Medium (generated stubs) |
| **Versioning** | URL / header | Schema evolution + field deprecation | Protobuf field numbers |
| **Rate limiting** | Per-endpoint simple | Complex (query cost) | Per-method |
| **Typical use** | Public APIs, simple | Complex frontends, mobile | Internal services |

sections.title: When to Pick Each — With Examples
sections.content:
**Pick REST when:**

- **Public API / B2B**: partners expect REST; curl-friendly; OpenAPI spec widely understood
- **Simple CRUD services**: Spring Data REST, @RestController — lowest friction
- **HTTP caching matters**: ETags, Cache-Control, CDN-friendly GETs
- **Mobile apps with simple data needs**: few queries; REST is fine
- **Team is new to microservices**: REST has the smallest learning curve

*Example:* E-commerce catalog service with `/products`, `/products/{id}`, `/categories`. Browsers, partners, CDN all benefit from standard REST.

**Pick GraphQL when:**

- **Mobile app with many screens, varying data needs**: one screen wants user + orders; another wants user + profile + preferences. Client specifies; server doesn't need one endpoint per screen.
- **BFF (Backend for Frontend)**: GraphQL aggregates data from many REST/gRPC services into a shape each frontend wants
- **Rapidly changing clients**: web + iOS + Android teams add fields without backend REST changes
- **Complex, nested resources**: social network (posts, comments, likes, users) with many traversals
- **Avoiding over-fetching for expensive fields**: computed fields only fetched when requested

*Example:* GitHub's API v4 is GraphQL. Single endpoint; clients request exactly `repositories { issues { comments } }` without 10 REST calls. Netflix, Shopify, Facebook heavy GraphQL users.

**Pick gRPC when:**

- **Internal service-to-service calls**: polyglot (Java, Go, Python, Node), type-safe stubs, HTTP/2 multiplexing
- **High RPC volume**: 100k+ req/sec — Protobuf + HTTP/2 far more efficient than JSON
- **Streaming**: live telemetry, chat, financial feeds — bidirectional natively
- **Strict latency budgets**: gRPC is 3–10× faster than equivalent REST
- **Schema-first team culture**: Protobuf in a shared repo; CI enforces compatibility

*Example:* Netflix's internal services heavily use gRPC. Google internal RPC is all gRPC. Uber, Lyft, Airbnb use it at scale.

**Hybrid: the 2026 reality**

```
Client (Browser / Mobile)
   |
   REST or GraphQL
   v
API Gateway / BFF
   |
   gRPC
   v
Internal Microservices
   |
   Events (Kafka)
   v
Background Workers
```

- REST at the edge for simple endpoints, public APIs
- GraphQL BFF for complex frontends
- gRPC between internal services
- Events for async decoupling

**Anti-patterns**

- **GraphQL for a simple CRUD app**: overkill; REST is simpler
- **gRPC for public API**: browsers struggle; partners don't have tooling
- **REST with huge chatty calls**: refactor to batch endpoint or introduce GraphQL BFF
- **Running GraphQL without DataLoader**: N+1 kills performance
- **Protobuf field renumbering**: breaks all clients; use reserved keyword

sections.title: Deep Trade-offs and Gotchas
sections.content:
**GraphQL N+1 problem.** A query like `posts { author { name } }` with 100 posts can execute 1 query for posts + 100 for authors = 101 queries. **DataLoader** (Facebook's batching library) buffers author IDs and fetches in one query. Critical for GraphQL performance; not optional.

**GraphQL query cost.** Client can write arbitrarily expensive queries (deeply nested, paginated in bad ways). Solutions: query complexity analysis (reject queries > X complexity), max depth limits (reject nesting > 7), persisted queries (only allow pre-registered query hashes), rate limit by complexity not request count.

**HTTP caching with GraphQL is hard.** POST with query body can't be CDN-cached. Solutions: persisted queries + GET with hash (CDN can cache); Apollo Response Cache; client-side normalized cache (Apollo Client, Relay).

**GraphQL over-simplifies schema evolution.** Deprecate fields via `@deprecated` directive; clients see warnings. Removing = breaking. Compatibility discipline is real.

**Apollo Federation vs REST microservices.** Federation lets multiple services each expose partial GraphQL schema; gateway stitches. Modern microservices pattern for GraphQL. Alternative: BFF pattern where one GraphQL server calls many REST/gRPC microservices.

**gRPC streaming shines for real-time.** Server-streaming: one request, many responses (stock ticker). Client-streaming: many requests, one response (upload chunks). Bidirectional: chat, telemetry. REST has SSE + WebSocket but less native.

**gRPC-Web limitations.** Browsers don't natively speak gRPC (HTTP/2 frame access limited). gRPC-Web uses a subset (no client streaming, limited bidirectional) + proxy (Envoy). Adds complexity.

**Protobuf schema evolution rules.**
- Adding fields: safe (new tag numbers with defaults)
- Removing fields: dangerous; reserve tag number (`reserved 5`)
- Renaming fields: safe (name is documentation; tag is wire)
- Renumbering: breaks wire compatibility; don't

**REST versioning strategies.**
- URL versioning: `/v1/users` vs `/v2/users` (explicit, common)
- Header versioning: `Accept: application/vnd.api.v2+json`
- Content negotiation: less common
- Evolution without versioning: add fields only, deprecate via headers

**HATEOAS in REST.** Hypermedia-driven API where responses include links to related actions. Elegant in theory, rare in practice. Most REST APIs are RPC-flavored. Don't over-engineer HATEOAS.

**REST batch endpoints.** Instead of one call per resource, offer `POST /batch` accepting an array. Alternative to GraphQL for simpler systems.

**GraphQL subscriptions (real-time).** Over WebSocket; server pushes to client when data changes. Different protocol than queries/mutations. Alternative to SSE.

**OpenAPI is REST's schema.** Generated docs (Swagger UI), client SDKs (openapi-generator), server stubs. Makes REST strongly-typed; many orgs skip this.

**gRPC with REST-like gateway.** grpc-gateway or Envoy can expose gRPC services as REST for browsers/partners. Best of both worlds; adds config complexity.

**Rate limiting.**
- REST: per endpoint, per IP/user simple
- GraphQL: by query cost/complexity (hard to calculate at gateway)
- gRPC: per method, per client; interceptors handle it

**Tracing and observability.**
- REST: standard (HTTP status, URL, method); every APM tool supports
- GraphQL: needs instrumentation per resolver; OpenTelemetry GraphQL extension
- gRPC: spans natively via interceptor; OpenTelemetry gRPC support is first-class

**Testing.**
- REST: MockMvc, RestAssured, Postman, contract testing (Pact, Spring Cloud Contract)
- GraphQL: @graphql-codegen, Apollo mocks, Mercurius
- gRPC: generated stubs mockable; contract testing via Pact (message-level) or Buf lint/breaking

**BFF pattern.** Backend For Frontend: one backend per client type (mobile, web, smart TV). Each BFF can use GraphQL to aggregate shared services. Netflix, Spotify popularized. Trade-off: more services to maintain, but each frontend gets optimal data shapes.

**Cost of change.**
- REST: add endpoint; update OpenAPI; clients regenerate or manually update
- GraphQL: add field to schema; existing clients unaffected; new clients use it
- gRPC: add field to Protobuf; recompile clients; binary compatibility within tag rules

**The 2026 default recommendations:**
- **Public API**: REST with OpenAPI (comfort, tooling, docs)
- **Internal microservices**: gRPC (efficiency, type safety)
- **Mobile/SPA BFF**: GraphQL (field selection, fewer round-trips)
- **Real-time**: gRPC bidirectional or WebSocket, not GraphQL subscriptions unless already on GraphQL
- **Mixed**: combine — REST at edge, gRPC internal, GraphQL BFF where complexity justifies

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **REST**: resource-based, ubiquitous, HTTP cache-friendly; best for public APIs, simple services
- **GraphQL**: client-specified fields, eliminates over/under-fetching; best for complex frontends, mobile BFF
- **gRPC**: HTTP/2 + Protobuf, binary, fast, polyglot; best for internal service-to-service
- **Over-fetching/under-fetching** is REST's core weakness; GraphQL solves this
- **N+1 problem is GraphQL's curse** — DataLoader is mandatory, not optional
- **HTTP caching works natively with REST**, breaks with GraphQL POST; persisted queries + GET help
- **gRPC-Web needs proxy for browsers** (Envoy); adds complexity
- **Protobuf schema discipline** — never renumber fields; reserve removed tags
- **Query complexity analysis** is GraphQL's rate-limiting answer
- **Hybrid architectures** are common: REST at edge, gRPC internal, GraphQL BFF

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Three dominant API styles in 2026, each with distinct sweet spots.

**REST over HTTP plus JSON — the ubiquitous default**
- Resource-based: URLs identify things, verbs act on them
- JSON is human-readable; tooling is everywhere
- HTTP semantics free: status codes, caching, content negotiation
- Schemas via OpenAPI, optional
- Scales from tiny to massive
- Downsides: verbose payloads, multiple round-trips for complex views, over-fetching (returns fields client doesn't need), under-fetching (missing nested data)

**GraphQL — Facebook's query language, open-sourced 2015**
- Single endpoint accepting a query
- Client specifies exactly what fields it wants, including nested
- One request returns exactly that shape
- Strong schema; introspection; rich tooling like GraphiQL and Apollo Studio
- Downsides: query cost unpredictable; N+1 problem without DataLoader; HTTP caching breaks (POST with body); server complexity; learning curve

**gRPC — Google, 2015**
- HTTP/2 plus Protobuf: binary, compact, 3 to 10x smaller than JSON
- Strongly typed; compiled stubs in multiple languages
- Four modes: unary, server streaming, client streaming, bidirectional
- Deadlines, metadata, interceptors
- Downsides: not browser-friendly without gRPC-Web proxy; harder debugging (binary wire); schema discipline required

**When to pick each**

*REST when*
- Public API or B2B partners
- Simple CRUD services
- HTTP caching matters
- Team new to microservices
- Lowest learning curve

*GraphQL when*
- Mobile app with many screens needing varying data
- BFF aggregating many services
- Rapidly changing clients (web, iOS, Android teams evolve independently)
- Complex nested resources
- Avoiding over-fetching expensive fields

*gRPC when*
- Internal service-to-service at high volume
- Polyglot teams needing type safety
- Streaming use cases: telemetry, chat, financial feeds
- Strict latency budgets
- Schema-first team culture

**The hybrid reality**
- REST at the edge for public APIs and simple endpoints
- GraphQL BFF for complex frontends
- gRPC between internal services
- Events on Kafka for async decoupling

**Key concepts**

*Over-fetching and under-fetching are REST's core weakness*
- REST returns whole resource; client uses 10% of fields
- Or client needs user plus orders plus items; three round trips
- GraphQL asks client to specify; eliminates both

*N+1 problem is GraphQL's curse*
- Query like 'posts { author { name } }' with 100 posts can run 101 queries
- DataLoader batches author lookups into one query
- Mandatory, not optional

*Query complexity analysis is GraphQL's rate-limiting answer*
- Client can write arbitrarily expensive queries
- Analyze complexity; reject beyond limit; max depth
- Persisted queries: only allow pre-registered query hashes from clients

*HTTP caching works with REST, breaks with GraphQL*
- GraphQL POST with body can't be CDN-cached
- Persisted queries plus GET with hash enable CDN caching
- Apollo Response Cache, client-side normalized cache (Apollo Client, Relay)

*Protobuf schema evolution discipline*
- Adding fields safe; removing dangerous; never renumber
- Reserve tag numbers for removed fields
- Schema in shared repo with CI breakage checks (Buf)

*gRPC-Web needs proxy*
- Browsers don't natively speak gRPC over HTTP/2 frame access
- Envoy proxy translates; gRPC-Web has subset (no client streaming)
- Adds moving piece but solvable

**Versioning approaches**
- REST: URL (/v1/users, /v2/users) or header-based; common
- GraphQL: schema evolution via @deprecated; no hard versions
- gRPC: Protobuf field numbers; additive evolution safe

**Tracing and observability**
- REST: standard; every APM supports
- GraphQL: needs per-resolver instrumentation; OpenTelemetry GraphQL extension
- gRPC: spans via interceptor; OpenTelemetry first-class support

**Anti-patterns**
- GraphQL for simple CRUD: overkill; REST simpler
- gRPC for public API: browsers struggle; partners lack tooling
- REST with chatty calls: introduce batch endpoint or GraphQL BFF
- GraphQL without DataLoader: N+1 kills performance
- Protobuf renumbering: breaks all clients

**The 2026 default recommendations**
- Public API: REST with OpenAPI
- Internal microservices: gRPC
- Mobile or SPA BFF: GraphQL
- Real-time: gRPC bidirectional or WebSocket
- Mixed architecture: combine all three, each where it fits

**The strategic answer**
- No religious war; pick based on use case
- REST for simplicity and ubiquity
- GraphQL for field-selection needs and BFF
- gRPC for internal performance and type safety
- Real systems combine all three; architecture matches where each excels

questions.question: REST vs WebSocket vs Server-Sent Events — which pattern for real-time features, and how do you choose?
questions.title: REST vs WebSocket vs SSE — Real-Time Pattern Decision
questions.direct_answer: Pick by the **direction and duration** of the data flow. Use **REST (+ long-polling)** when updates are sparse and clients are numerous — simplest, cache-friendly, stateless. Use **Server-Sent Events (SSE)** when the server pushes one-way updates to a browser or HTTP client — feed-style notifications, dashboards, LLM token streaming; it's just HTTP, cache-hostile but firewall-friendly, auto-reconnects, carries `Last-Event-ID`. Use **WebSockets** when you need **full-duplex low-latency** messaging — chat, collaborative editing, trading — but accept the stateful connection, custom auth, and horizontal-scaling cost. In 2026, gRPC streaming and HTTP/3 server push nibble at both edges; default to SSE for one-way server→client and WebSocket only when the client must push back in real time.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can match a real-time requirement (notification, chat, dashboard, stock ticker, AI streaming) to the right protocol, and articulate the operational cost of each choice — stateful vs stateless, auth shape, reconnection behaviour, horizontal scaling.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reaching for WebSockets for every 'real-time' requirement — incurring sticky sessions, Redis pub/sub fan-out, and custom auth — when one-way SSE would be simpler and cheaper. Also the reverse: building long-polling for a collaborative editor where WebSockets are the obvious fit.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss SSE's `Last-Event-ID` resumption, WebSocket frame types and close codes, the STOMP/MQTT-over-WebSocket framing option, how HTTP/2 multiplexing interacts with SSE, sticky-session requirements for WebSocket scaling, and where gRPC bidirectional streaming and HTTP/3 server push displace both.

sections.title: Three Protocols, Three Shapes of Data Flow
sections.content:
Real-time is a marketing word; the engineering question is always **who pushes data to whom, how often, and for how long**. Three patterns cover 95% of cases.

- **REST with polling / long-polling** — the client pulls on a schedule; long-polling holds a request open until the server has something to say. Stateless, cache-friendly, works through every proxy, degrades gracefully. Cost: latency floor equals poll interval; at scale you burn capacity on empty responses.
- **Server-Sent Events (SSE)** — a single HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 response that never closes; the server writes `data:` frames as it pleases and the browser (or any HTTP client) dispatches them as events. One-way only. Auto-reconnect with `Last-Event-ID` is built into `EventSource`. Perfect for notifications, dashboards, progress streams, and LLM token streaming.
- **WebSocket (RFC 6455)** — a TCP-like full-duplex channel over an HTTP upgrade. Binary or text frames, either side can write at any time. The right tool for chat, collaborative editing, gaming, trading. Cost: the connection is stateful, auth happens once at upgrade (or via subprotocols like STOMP), and horizontal scaling needs sticky sessions or a shared message bus.

Two newer entrants are displacing the edges:
- **gRPC bidirectional streaming** over HTTP/2 for internal service-to-service real-time — better types, built-in deadlines, but not browser-native without gRPC-Web
- **HTTP/3 server push and QUIC streams** lower the handshake cost of both polling and SSE; not yet a full WebSocket replacement

sections.title: Side-by-Side Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | REST (+ long-poll) | Server-Sent Events | WebSocket |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Direction** | Client pull | Server → client only | Full-duplex |
| **Transport** | HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 request-response | HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 streaming response | HTTP upgrade to TCP frames |
| **Stateful connection** | No (each request) | Yes (single open response) | Yes (until close) |
| **Auth** | Standard HTTP (Bearer, cookie) | Standard HTTP (Bearer, cookie) | Custom at upgrade (subprotocols, tokens in first frame) |
| **Proxy & firewall** | Works everywhere | Works almost everywhere (just HTTP) | Often blocked by corporate proxies; needs WSS |
| **Reconnect** | No — next request | Automatic (`EventSource` + `Last-Event-ID`) | Manual (reconnect + resubscribe) |
| **Message types** | Request/response (JSON, XML) | Text events with `event:`, `id:`, `retry:` | Text or binary frames |
| **Ordering & framing** | Per request | Per event line | Per frame |
| **Scales horizontally** | Trivial (stateless) | Moderate (sticky-ish; Redis pub-sub for fan-out) | Hard (sticky sessions + shared bus) |
| **Back-pressure** | Natural (poll interval) | TCP-level | TCP-level; app must throttle |
| **Caching** | CDN-friendly | Not cacheable | Not cacheable |
| **Browser API** | `fetch` | `EventSource` | `WebSocket` |
| **Typical use** | CRUD, low-frequency updates | Notifications, dashboards, LLM streaming | Chat, collab editing, trading, gaming |
| **Cost per idle client** | ~0 | One open HTTP response + heap | One open TCP + WS state |

sections.title: Three Clients, Side by Side
Spring Boot — SSE vs WebSocket Endpoint
Operational Shape — Auth, Reconnect, Scale
sections.content:
**Auth** - REST and SSE reuse standard HTTP auth (Bearer, cookie, mTLS).
- No custom logic needed; CSRF rules apply to cookie-based auth on SSE
- WebSocket upgrades happen with HTTP, so cookies and bearer tokens survive the upgrade — but only the first request carries them.
- Token refresh mid-connection is a custom protocol problem
- Never put tokens in query strings for WebSocket — server-side access logs and intermediaries capture them

**Reconnection and resumption** - REST long-polling — reconnect is the next request; carry `?cursor=...` for gap-free delivery
- SSE — `EventSource` auto-reconnects; browser sends `Last-Event-ID` header so the server can replay missed events.
- Implement it; otherwise the reconnect just restarts the stream
- WebSocket — you own reconnect.
- Implement exponential backoff, resubscribe on open, and a sequence number or ack protocol for at-least-once delivery

**Horizontal scaling** - REST — trivial; any instance serves any request
- SSE — mostly stateless per connection but each open connection pins to an instance.
- Use a shared bus (Redis pub-sub, Kafka, NATS) so any instance can publish events that reach all subscribers
- WebSocket — sticky sessions (usually via a load balancer with cookie/session hash), **plus** the same shared bus.
- Dropping a node disconnects clients; graceful-shutdown requires draining with GOAWAY-like semantics

**Resource cost per idle client**
- REST — zero between polls
- SSE — one open HTTP response; a server-thread-per-client model (Tomcat default) caps out around 10k; WebFlux on Netty comfortably handles 100k+
- WebSocket — one open TCP + frame buffers + application session; similar scaling profile to SSE on Netty, much worse on thread-per-request

**Observability**
- REST — standard `http.server.requests` metrics
- SSE — export `sse.active.connections`, per-event throughput, reconnect rate; track `Last-Event-ID` gap as a quality signal
- WebSocket — active sessions, frames per second, close codes histogram (1000/1001 normal, 1006 abnormal — page the team when 1006 spikes)

sections.title: Picking the Right Pattern — Concrete Scenarios
sections.content:
**Order status page updating every few minutes** → REST polling every 10–30 s, or webhooks pushing from a message bus. Over-engineering this with WebSockets is the single most common mistake.

**Notification bell, live dashboards, activity feed** → **SSE**. One-way, firewall-friendly, auto-reconnect, browser-native. Scale via Redis pub-sub for fan-out.

**LLM streaming tokens** → **SSE**. OpenAI, Anthropic, and every major LLM vendor expose streaming over SSE — matches the one-way pattern and is dead simple on the client (`EventSource` or `fetch` with `ReadableStream`).

**Chat, collaborative editing (Figma, Google Docs, Notion)** → **WebSocket**, often with a CRDT protocol over the frames. Both sides push; bidirectional is the point.

**Stock ticker / trading feed** → WebSocket for retail, gRPC streaming or custom TCP for institutional. SSE is viable for read-only public feeds.

**Multiplayer game state sync** → WebSocket for browser, UDP/QUIC for native clients. The low-latency bidirectional requirement is non-negotiable.

**IoT telemetry → backend** → MQTT is usually right; WebSocket is an acceptable fallback when MQTT ports are blocked.

**Server-to-service real-time inside your own infra** → **gRPC bidirectional streaming**. Strong types, deadlines, auth via mTLS; better than WebSocket for this shape.

**Mobile push notifications** → Platform push (APNs, FCM) — don't roll your own; background connections are unreliable on mobile.

sections.title: Trade-offs and Common Mistakes
sections.content:
**When SSE is underrated**
- One-way server-push covers most "real-time" requirements in web apps
- HTTP semantics mean standard auth, observability, and CDN edge termination all just work
- Failure mode is graceful — browser reconnects automatically with `Last-Event-ID`

**When WebSocket is overkill**
- Notifications, dashboards, progress updates, LLM streaming, log tails — all one-way; SSE is simpler to build, debug, and scale
- Any scenario where the client talks to the server only via explicit user actions — regular HTTP is enough

**When WebSocket is the only correct answer**
- Sub-100-ms round-trip from client → server and back, continuously
- Both sides send messages independently (chat, collab, gaming)
- Binary payloads with their own framing (WebRTC signalling, custom protocols)

**Common anti-patterns**
- Opening a WebSocket per tab per page just for notifications → SSE is cheaper and simpler
- Using HTTP short polling every 500 ms → paying for thousands of empty requests per minute; long-poll or SSE
- Putting tokens in the WebSocket URL query string → leaks into logs, NAT tables, histories
- No heartbeat on WebSocket — zombie connections linger after NAT timeout; send a ping/pong every 30 s
- Ignoring `Last-Event-ID` for SSE resumption — reconnect drops events silently
- Sticky sessions without a shared bus — node failure disconnects clients and they resubscribe to a different node that never sees their events

**Edges being displaced**
- Internal service-to-service real-time → gRPC bidi streaming almost always wins over WebSocket (types, deadlines, proto-generated clients)
- One-way LLM streaming → SSE is the de facto standard; HTTP/3 server push exists but SSE interop dominates
- Long-polling for APIs → webhooks when the receiver is a server, SSE when it is a browser

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Direction decides the protocol** — client pulls (REST), server pushes one-way (SSE), both sides push (WebSocket / gRPC streaming)
- **Default to SSE for notifications, dashboards, LLM streaming** — simpler than WebSocket, reuses HTTP auth and observability, auto-reconnect via `Last-Event-ID`
- **WebSocket earns its complexity only when the client must push back in real time** — chat, collab, gaming, trading
- **REST long-polling remains viable** for sparse updates with many clients — stateless, CDN-friendly, cheapest per idle client
- **Scaling SSE and WebSocket needs a shared bus** (Redis pub-sub, Kafka, NATS) so any instance can publish; WebSocket additionally needs sticky sessions
- **Token-in-URL is an anti-pattern for WebSockets** — use cookies, `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, or first-frame auth
- **Close-code 1006 spike is your paging signal** — abnormal WebSocket closes indicate network or server-side failures
- **gRPC bidirectional streaming displaces WebSocket for service-to-service** — strong types, deadlines, mTLS; keep WebSocket for browser clients

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The protocol depends on who pushes data to whom and how often.

**REST with polling or long-polling**
- Stateless, CDN-friendly, works through every proxy
- Right for sparse updates with many clients — order status updating every few minutes, low-frequency dashboards
- Latency floor is the poll interval; long-polling closes the gap at the cost of open connections

**Server-Sent Events**
- A single HTTP response that never closes; server writes `data:` frames as events
- One-way only — server to client
- Reuses HTTP auth, works through firewalls, and `EventSource` auto-reconnects carrying `Last-Event-ID` so the server can replay missed events
- My default for notifications, live dashboards, progress streams, and LLM token streaming
- Scales by pinning each connection to a node plus a shared bus like Redis pub-sub for fan-out

**WebSocket**
- Full-duplex; either side can send frames at any time
- Right for chat, collaborative editing, trading, gaming — anywhere the client must push back in real time
- Cost: stateful, needs sticky sessions for horizontal scale, custom reconnect and resubscription logic, custom auth beyond the handshake
- Watch close-code 1006 in metrics — it's the abnormal close signal

**When I reach for each**
- Notifications, dashboards, LLM streaming → SSE
- Chat, collab, gaming, trading → WebSocket
- CRUD with occasional real-time needs → REST plus a webhook or long-poll
- Internal service-to-service streaming → gRPC bidirectional, not WebSocket

**Common mistakes**
- Defaulting to WebSocket for everything labelled "real-time" — one-way notifications want SSE
- Short-polling every 500 ms — burn capacity on empty responses
- Putting tokens in the WebSocket URL — leaks into logs
- No shared bus behind scaled SSE/WebSocket — one node can't deliver events produced by another

**2026 context**
- gRPC bidirectional streaming is the right answer for internal service-to-service, not WebSocket
- HTTP/3 lowers handshake cost of both polling and SSE
- SSE has quietly won the LLM-streaming space; the industry moved away from custom WebSocket protocols there

beats.text: Real-time is a marketing word; the engineering question is always who pushes data to whom, how often, and for how long. Three patterns cover 95% of cases. REST with polling / long-polling — the client pulls on a schedule; long-polling holds a request open until the server has something to say. Stateless, cache-friendly, works through every proxy, degrades gracefully. Cost: latency floor equals poll interval; at scale you burn capacity.
